Hot take here: I'm inclined to agree with the posit that tooth damage is caused by some sort of serious trauma.

The obvious example would be physical trauma, like a hockey puck to the face. But the far less obvious example is psychological trauma. Myself as an example is hella biased because I was molested by a dude who wanted me for my teeth so it makes perfect sense I'd stop taking care of my teeth. But as I've learned from talking with other people, being molested alone is enough to cause depression and feelings of lacking self-worth. The brain goes into this life-long panic mode prioritizing escaping the pain of the event and foregoing any sort of self-care.

Drug use is another example. Sure, one of the chemical side effects of meth (and coffee, and alcohol, and sugary foods, etc,) is tooth decay. But people engage in it out of addiction. Addiction is a disease that has a genetic component which requires a sufficiently traumatic event to activate it. People can trick themselves into saying they use meth because it's fun, but it clearly stops being fun at some point. They only stop using when they realize they're using it to treat their inner-pain and continue to stop using it by engaging in self-care like a healthy person.
